Question: Let \(n\) be the number of ways that \(10\) dollars can be changed into dimes and quarters, with at least one of each coin being used. Then \(n\) equals:
Solution:
Let \(d\) and \(q\) be the numbers of dimes and quarters. Since ten dollars is \(1000\) cents,
\[
10d+25q=1000,
\qquad 2d+5q=200.
\]
The numbers \(2d\) and \(200\) are even, so \(5q\) must be even. Because \(5\) is odd, \(q\) must be even. Write \(q=2k\), where \(k\) is an integer. The equation then gives
\[
d=100-5k.
\]
Both types of coin must be used, so \(k>0\) and \(100-5k>0\). Thus
\[
k=1,2,\ldots,19.
\]
Every one of these values produces positive integer coin counts totaling ten dollars. Conversely, every allowed combination has exactly one such value of \(k\), so none is omitted or counted twice. Therefore \(n=\boxed{19}\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
